images.title: Two glasses in twentieths
images.purpose: Show that 3/4 and 7/10 can be compared once both shares are written in twentieths: 15/20 is more than 14/20.
images.composition: Two tall straight-sided juice glasses standing side by side on one baseline with wide space between them, and one comparison line centred below.
images.exact_structure: Left: one tall straight-sided glass drawn as a plain upright rectangle, marked inside by thin grey #6B7280 lines into 20 equal levels; the bottom 15 levels filled teal #0072B2. Right: one glass of exactly the same size on the same baseline, also marked into 20 equal levels; the bottom 14 levels filled amber #E69F00. One thin dashed reddish purple #CC79A7 horizontal line across both glasses at the top of the teal fill. Centred below: one comparison line. Exactly 2 glasses, 20 levels each, 15 teal, 14 amber.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
glasses of different sizes, tapered glasses, or levels that are not equal
images.takeaway: When the children differ, make the units the same first, then compare.
images.description: Two same-size glasses each marked in 20 equal levels: 15 teal levels show 3/4 = 15/20 and 14 amber levels show 7/10 = 14/20, so the group of 4 children gets more.
images.context: Shown with the concept as its one key picture, next to the walkthrough video. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not generated yet.
images.teaching_notes: Ask the student to count the levels above the amber fill up to the purple line and say who gets more juice.

image_decisions.why: Two glasses in the same twentieths make a close comparison visible at a glance.
